title: Building pi in a World of Slop — Mario Zechner

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk's primary focus is building pi, a minimal self-modifying agent harness, and critiquing agent harness architecture including context management, tool design, and harness extensibility. Pi is a coding agent harness for software builders and is also embedded as the agentic core of OpenClaw, a developer platform tool. Pi is deployed and scored on Terminal Bench, and the talk extensively covers production realities of agent-driven development including OSS maintenance and operational complexity. Requires familiarity with coding agent harnesses, context management, and software engineering practices but is accessible to practitioners without deep ML expertise. This is a recorded conference talk with structured sections and demonstrations. All claims are directly stated in the transcript with supporting evidence anchors.

summary: Mario Zechner's talk traces his journey from frustrated Claude Code user to creator of pi, a self-modifying agent harness, then pivots to a broader critique of agent-driven software development. Act 1 covers his dissatisfaction with Claude Code controlling context behind his back—system prompts and tool definitions changing every release, system reminders confusing models, no observability, model choice, or deep extensibility. He surveyed alternatives: Amp and FactoryDroid as premium options, Open Code as OSS but flawed (pruning tool outputs, injecting LSP errors, insecure CORS defaults). Terminal Bench revealed that minimal harnesses (Terminus with just tmux tools) outperform feature-rich ones, inspiring pi: a minimal core with four tools (read, write, edit, bash), near-empty system prompt, and TypeScript extensions with hot reload. YOLO security gives users rope rather than gating actions. Pi scored 6th on Terminal Bench's October leaderboard. Act 2 covers collateral damage: Peter embedded pi as OpenClaw's agentic core, making Mario's OSS project a target for 'clankers' flooding issue trackers. He auto-closes PRs, deprioritizes interacted issues, visualizes issue clusters in 3D, and invented 'OS certification' (closing the tracker to reclaim his life). Act 3 is a plea to slow down. Agents compound 'booboos' (errors) with zero learning, no bottlenecks, and delayed pain for humans. Models learned complexity from internet garbage code, producing enterprise-grade complexity within two weeks. Specs with blanks get filled with mediocre learned patterns. Review agents create an 'ouroboros' that catches some issues but can't fix systemic complexity. Humans, while fallible, can learn, feel pain, and are natural bottlenecks—agents happily keep shoveling code. Long context windows are a hack; agentic search fails; agents patch locally and break globally. You can't trust your codebase or tests if agents wrote them. His practical advice: scope tasks so agents find everything needed, modularize code, provide evaluation functions, let agents handle non-mission-critical boring tasks and reproduction cases, cap generated code for review, read every line of critical code, and hand-write anything important. Friction builds understanding. Discipline, agency, and humans remain essential.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Intro and motivation
sections.summary: Mario introduces the talk as a tragedy in three acts, mentions torso ad space proceeds going to charity, and previews the structure.

sections.title: Act 1: Frustration with Claude Code
sections.summary: Mario describes starting with Claude Code in April 2025, its initial appeal, and growing frustration as features brought bugs and context was controlled behind his back—system prompts and tool definitions change every release, system reminders confuse the model, and there is no observability, model choice, or deep extensibility.

sections.title: Surveying alternatives and Open Code issues
sections.summary: He evaluates Amp and FactoryDroid as premium options and Open Code as OSS, finding Open Code's context handling problematic: pruning tool outputs (lobotomizing the model), injecting LSP errors after each edit (confusing the model), storing each message as a separate JSON file, and shipping insecure CORS defaults that expose the server to any browser tab.

sections.title: Terminal Bench and minimal harness insight
sections.summary: Terminal Bench shows Terminus—a minimal tmux-only harness with no file tools or sub-agents—outperforming feature-rich native harnesses irrespective of model family, suggesting agents are in an 'around and find out' phase needing self-modifying malleable forms.

sections.title: Introducing pi
sections.summary: Pi's architecture: four packages (AI abstraction, agent core while-loop, bespoke TUI framework, coding agent), near-empty system prompt since models are reinforcement-trained as coding agents, four tools (read, write, edit, bash), and self-modification via shipped documentation and code examples.

sections.title: YOLO security and extensibility
sections.summary: YOLO philosophy gives rope instead of gating; extensions are TypeScript modules with hot reload; no sub-agents, plan mode, or MCP built in but can be added by asking pi; extensions shareable via NPM/GitHub without new marketplaces.

sections.title: Extension examples and Terminal Bench result
sections.summary: Examples include chat rooms for pi agents, NES games, and Doom extensions. Pi scored 6th on Terminal Bench's October leaderboard before compaction was added. Mario urges the audience to retake control of their tools and workflows.

sections.title: Act 2: Clankers destroying OSS
sections.summary: Peter embedded pi as OpenClaw's agentic core, turning Mario's OSS project into a target for automated agent instances ('clankers') flooding issue trackers with garbage. Till Draw closed their tracker; half of Mario's is OpenClaw noise. He auto-closes PRs, deprioritizes interacted issues, visualizes clusters in 3D, and invented 'OS certification'—closing the tracker to reclaim his life.

sections.title: Act 3: Plea to slow down—agents as error-compounding complexity generators
sections.summary: Mario argues agents compound 'booboos' (errors) with zero learning, no bottlenecks, and delayed pain for humans. Models learned complexity from 90% garbage internet code, producing enterprise-grade complexity within two weeks. Specs with blanks get filled with mediocre patterns. Review agents create an 'ouroboros' that catches some issues but can't fix systemic complexity. Humans, while fallible, learn and feel pain—making them essential bottlenecks.

sections.title: Act 3 continued: Why long context and agentic search fail
sections.summary: Long context windows are a hack and agentic search is failing. Agents patch locally and break globally. You can't trust your codebase or tests if agents wrote them. When users scream, you haven't read the code, and agents are overwhelmed by the humongous codebase with insufficient context.

sections.title: Act 3: Practical advice for working with agents
sections.summary: Good agent tasks need tight scope, modularized code, and evaluation functions. Let agents handle non-mission-critical boring tasks and reproduction cases. Cap generated code for review. Read every line of critical code; hand-write anything important. Friction builds system understanding. Learn to say no. Fewer features that matter, polished by agents. Discipline, agency, and humans remain essential.
